entries.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy in UK to meet new PM Burnham
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy traveled to Portsmouth for UK PM Andy Burnham's first meeting with a foreign leader since taking office. The UK pledged "unwavering support" in Ukraine's ongoing defense against Russia.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine's Zelenskyy in UK to meet new PM Burnham

July 27, 2026

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy traveled to Portsmouth for UK PM Andy Burnham's first meeting with a foreign leader since taking office. The UK pledged "unwavering support" in Ukraine's ongoing defense against Russia.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the UK on Monday where he and new prime minister Andy Burnhamdiscussed continued defense cooperation. The two visited some 200 Ukrainian service members training with UK troops at Portsmouth Naval Base.

The Ukrainian forces have been sharpening their war-fighting and countermining measures for operations in the Black Sea.

Speaking in Portsmouth, Burnham said, "Volodymyr, you are the first leader I have welcomed in person since taking office and that is no accident."

"It is intended to send a very clear message," the new prime minister added, "We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honor every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."

Posting on X after the meeting, Zelenskyy wrote: "We greatly appreciate that our team is the first to visit the United Kingdom since Andy Burnham took office. This is an important signal of support, and the Prime Minister assured us that this support remains unwavering."

UK providing new radar jamming technology to aid deep strike capabilities

Burnham announced that the UK is now providing Kyiv with access to its "Stone Cloak" electronic jamming technology, with thousands of the jammers already given to Kyiv according to Downing Street.

When affixed to drones, the battle-tested, tablet-sized Stone Cloak jammers can shield weapons from Russian air-defense systems detection, providing Kyiv with more lethal long-distance strike capabilities.

"Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries," Burnham said.

The deal comes as Ukraine has shifted from a purely defensive posture and increased its attacks on sites deep within Russia, notably its targeting of oil, military and logistics installations.

On Sunday, Zelenskyy told UK broadcaster Sky News that he hopes to sign a strong "drone deal" with Burnham to boost drone production capacity and technology sharing, adding, "we don't have enough missiles" to defend against Russia's continued air attacks.

Russia, said Zelenskyy, "can increase the production of ballistic missile missiles and that's why we need air defense as soon as possible."

UK support for Kyiv continues despite a revolving cast of prime ministers

Zelenskyy's visit is Burnham's first bilateral meeting with a foreign leader since taking over at Downing Street last week and comes as the Ukrainian prepares to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington on Tuesday.

Burnham assured Zelenskyy of the UK's "unwavering support" as Kyiv defends itself against a more than four-year Russian invasion.

"Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering," according to a statement.

"Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve, and we will not back down until we achieve long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine."

Zelenskyy described ties with the UK as "the strongest relationship in the entire history" of the two nations.

Prior to the meeting, Downing Street said Burnham — the fifth prime minister that Zelenskyy has dealt with since Russia launched its unprovoked full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022 — would pledge "to continue the unbreakable bond between the two nations."

Downing Street on Monday said that the UK had provided some 25 billion pounds (€29 billion ,$33 billion) in assistance to Ukraine since the war began, 16 billion of which were given in direct military assistance.

Next, Zelenskyy will seek support from Trump, who is mired in his own war with Iran

From the UK, Zelenskyy will travel to Washington, where he will meet with US President Trump at the White House on Tuesday.

Support from Trump, who is currently bogged down in his own war with Iran, has wavered during his time in office and the two leaders have had a famously contentious relationship.

Trump did, however, recently announce that Kyiv could be given permission to build US Patriot missile systems as Russian air assaults continue unabated.

In his Sunday Sky News interview, Zelenskyy expressed understanding for Trump's predicament, saying, "I understand the United States is focussing on the Middle East," adding that he would, "try to manage it [the war in Ukraine] with some Europeans and with Americans and with some other countries."

"This," he said, is "a big challenge," both for himself and for Ukraine.

Zelenskyy did get an important bit of assistance from lawmakers in Washington recently when Congress advanced bipartisan legislation targeting countries purchasing Russian energy, potentially making it harder for the Kremlin and President Vladimir Putin to finance its ongoing war.

While in Washington, Zelenskyy is also expected to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a key proponent of US support for Ukraine who died unexpectedly earlier this month after returning from Kyiv.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Chad's government says it's withdrawing from the ICC
entries.summary: Chad's Foreign Ministry has announced plans to leave the International Criminal Court. It said that its effectiveness was "limited and uneven." Chad's leader is a military officer accused of repressing the opposition.
entries.content:
Chad

Chad's government says it's withdrawing from the ICC

July 27, 2026

Chad's Foreign Ministry has announced plans to leave the International Criminal Court. It said that its effectiveness was "limited and uneven." Chad's leader is a military officer accused of repressing the opposition.

Chad's Foreign Ministry issued a statement on Monday saying that it had notified the UN Secretary General of its intention to withdraw from the Rome Statute, the international accord underpinning the International Criminal Court (ICC). 

Chad is the fourth francophone African country whose government is very closely linked to its miltary to take such a step in less than a year — following the coordinated exit by the juntas running Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger last September. 

The ICC prosecutes individuals for war crimes and crimes against humanity; it began operating in 2002.

What did Chad's government say about the ICC pullout?

The Foreign Ministry said that its decision followed "an in-depth review of the functioning of the International Criminal Court since it began operating in 2002 and of its record, whose effectiveness remains limited and uneven across different regions."

It said the court's own record of prosecutions revealed an "undeniable and egregious selectivity in principle, whether or not this selectivity is desired or subjected."

The statement then listed the ICC investigations launched since the court's founding, saying that nine of 13 cases concerned African states, while only four applied to other regions of the world and were "without any concrete progress" as yet.

It said that of seven individuals detained as a result of ICC investigations, only one hailed from a situation beyond the African continent.

The Foreign Ministry alleged that this demonstrated a lasting concentration of ICC cases focused on "the Global South in general and the African continent in particular." Chad also appealed to other African Union members to follow in its footsteps.

"This irrevocable decision by Chad in no way constitues a renunication of the moral imperative to provide justice to victims; rather, it reflects the conviction that national judicial systems and African judicial mechanisms are fully capable of carrying out this mission with dignity," the statement, signed by Foreign Ministry spokesperson Ibrahim Adam Mahamat, concluded.

What did Chad say about the US role in this move?

Last Thursday, Chad's Foreign Ministry had also raised the issue of the ICC.

In a statement after talks between a Chadian minister and a US official for Africa, Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia Jr., the government in N'Djamena said the US had urged it to reconsider its ICC membership.

"The US side expressed its concerns about the functionality of this institution and desired that Chad reexamine its commitment to the Rome Statute," the ministry wrote. Chad said that it "indicated that this request would be examined by the responsible authorities."

The withdrawal coincides with last week's vote to dimiss the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

The US, like Russia and several other countries, never ratified the Rome Statute and fully signed up to the ICC. However, past administrations in Washington had been broadly supportive of the court's work.

This has changed in particular since the ICC's issued arrest warrants against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defense minister, soon after Donald Trump won a second term in office in November 2024. The second Trump administration has often been critical both of the independent ICC and the UN more generally, under whose auspices the Rome Statute mechanism was negotiated. 

Why might Chad and President Mahamat Idriss Deby fear the ICC?

While Chad now has a nominally civilian government, the same family with close ties to the military has been in charge for more than 35 years.

Former President Idriss Deby came to power in a military coup in late 1990. He was in office for more than 30 years before the news of his death in April 2021. According to Chadian accounts, the former general died fighting on the front lines against an insurgency in the north of the country, just a day after news of his election victory for a sixth consecutive term had been announced after a vote marked by protests and widespread arrests.

His son, another officer, Mahamat Idriss Deby, was named the head of a transitional military council after Deby's death, with the government disbanded.

In October 2022, he extended his interim mandate, prompting public protests that were violently suppressed. Dozens were killed and several opposition parties were banned in response. 

By 2024, after a constitutional referendum, Mahamat Deby did stand in presidential elections. The main challenger still permitted to run was his own prime minsiter, Succes Masra, who had returned from exile in the US earlier that year. Deby the younger won with 60.1% of the vote, albeit with Masra and other opposition groups disputing the results.  Masra was arrested in May 2025, accused of inciting hatred amid violent clashes the government defined as an "attempted coup." He was sentenced to 20 years in prison last August. 

Chad is still fighting an insurgency lasting roughly a decade in the north of the country led by two groups with rear bases in southern Libya. It also faces an influx of refugees from Sudan's civil war and various other soures of domestic unrest.

The three other West African nations to pull out of the ICC last September — Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger — are all under supposedly interim leadership by military juntas after a 2020 coup in Mali, a 2022 takeover in Burkina Faso and a 2023 coup in Niger.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: German Chancellor Merz completes cabinet resuffle
entries.summary: After days of confusion, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reshuffled his cabinet. Conservative politicians fear that this will not help with the prospects in the upcoming state elections.
entries.content:
Germany

German Chancellor Merz completes cabinet resuffle

July 27, 2026

After days of confusion, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has reshuffled his cabinet. Conservative politicians fear that this will not help with the prospects in the upcoming state elections.

On Monday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) was finally able to announce the name of the new Federal Minister of Transport in Berlin, following a weekend of speculation and debate. Steffen Bilger (CDU), aged 47 — who previously served as a state secretary in the transport ministry from 2018 to 2021 — is stepping up to lead the ministry.

The Chancellor had criticized the outgoing Transport Minister, Patrick Schnieder (CDU), for doing too little to address the chronic chaos and frequent delays plaguing the Deutsche Bahn railway system. Merz also faulted him for initiating too few projects to improve Germany's ailing infrastructure.

On Monday, Merz said he expected the new minister to ensure that "we become faster and better at driving a new era of progress in Germany."

Bilger's appointment marks the latest step in a cabinet reshuffle of the conservative wing of the government. This chain reaction of personnel changes was triggered by the resignation of Jens Spahn — the powerful leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in the Bundestag — who was forced to step down following allegations of hypocrisy over his decision to have a child via surrogacy in the United States, circumventing German law and in violation of his party's principles.

Thorsten Frei: a Merz confidant

Thorsten Frei, previously the head of the chancellery, is now set to become the new leader of the conservative parliamentary group on Wednesday, which involves the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU). The 208 CDU and CSU lawmakers must cut their summer holidays short to vote on this appointment.

The 52-year-old Frei, currently serving as head of the chancellery and considered a close confidant of Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is now set to take over one of the most important positions in German politics. His task will be to explain his party's positions in speeches in the Bundestag and interviews with the media. Above all, he will have to secure majorities for the government's policies and negotiate with the conservatives' coalition partner, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

Nina Warken: a woman in a key position

Merz has a reputation for trusting only men within his inner circle. Now, 47-year-old Nina Warken — a politician from the wealthy southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg — is taking over from Frei and will manage the chancellery and be responsible for aligning the government's overall policy agenda.

Warken is a member of the women's organization of the Christian Democratic Union. As health minister, she had recently pushed through a cost-cutting program for statutory health insurance funds.

The chancellor considers Warken to be assertive and well-versed in security policy issues — an important quality, given that the head of the chancellery also coordinates oversight of Germany's intelligence agencies.

Carsten Linnemann: a health minister with a business focus

With Warken now leaving the health portfolio, Carsten Linnemann — previously the CDU general secretary — is set to take over.

Pundits argue that the chancellor certainly has a clear vision of how Linnemann should lead the department. Until now, Linnemann has been known primarily as an economics expert — a background that Friedrich Merz believes will serve him well in the new role: "Carsten Linnemann is taking over a ministry that represents the fastest-growing sector of our economy. The entire sector — which, unfortunately, we all too often view merely as a cost factor — is a vital part of our social fabric."

CDU politicians fear for September election prospects

Approval of the government's performance is at an all-time low. State elections are scheduled for September in three eastern states where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to see significant gains.

It is against this backdrop that Merz is demonstrating decisiveness.

"I assume that things will have calmed down somewhat by September," Merz said.

Sven Schulze (CDU), a minister in the Saxony-Anhalt state government, takes a very different view. Speaking to public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk on Monday, Schulze said the past few days had dominated political discussions and "not exactly gone well."

He added that it was almost impossible to focus on state-level issues during door-to-door campaigning in his state.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Indian youth score a win over Modi with humor and grit
entries.summary: Driven by social media satire, the Gen-Z-led "Cockroach" protest movement spurned by grievances over an exam scandal caused a shake-up in India's government. DW spoke with a few protesters in New Delhi.
entries.content:
India

Indian youth score a win over Modi with humor and grit

July 27, 2026

Driven by social media satire, the Gen-Z-led "Cockroach" protest movement spurned by grievances over an exam scandal caused a shake-up in India's government. DW spoke with a few protesters in New Delhi.

Walking from Jantar Mantar to Connaught Place in central New Delhi on Saturday evening provided an unusual sight for the prime corridor of power in the world's largest democracy.

Satirical posters mocking India's legislative, executive and judiciary were plastered on the walls, and the pavement was sprayed with sometimes "vulgar" graffiti mocking Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

These were all remnants of thousands of young Cockroach movement protesters who had flooded the streets hours earlier after India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.

Celebrating Pradhan's resignation, which had been a core protest demand, some protesters were heard telling security officials "see you at the next protest," coming only days after several people were injured in clashes with baton-wielding police who fired tear gas into crowds.

Instagram was also full of images from cities across India with young people dancing in front of police officials to the line "Everybody knows that I'm a good girl, officer " from Lana Del Ray's song "Playing Dangerous."

Others held posters reading: "Cuff me, daddy" and some were seen climbing atop police barricades.

India's Gen Z rattles government into change

The movement, known as the Cockroach Janta Party movement (CJP), came after the chief justice of India referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark. The name is also a play on Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Since a scandal broke in May involving a highly competitive university entrance exam, the Gen Z protests have spread across India, challenging the political establishment with Instagram reels, viral trends, sarcastic jingles and posters.

"In our generation humor has become the defense mechanism from pain, frustration and helplessness. This entire protest is driven by humor, driven by Instagram and social media," Karan Azad, a 24-year-old law student, told DW at the Jantar Mantar protest site in New Delhi.

Another protester held a sign addressed to Modi reading in transliterated Hindi: "Buddy, you can't even make tea," alluding to Modi's boyhood days as a tea seller.

"I had to do my part. I am the youth. If we don't stand up for ourselves no one else will, we have to fight this battle ourselves," the female protester with the sign told DW without giving her name.

A protester named Tushar, also 24, said he wasn't "afraid of a backlash" from the authorities, but rather "would have had FOMO [fear of missing out]" had he not joined the protest.

Ridhima, a 17-year-old school student, said: "If not us then who? Those who are not here, it just speaks to their cowardice and I am talking about people who are sitting on their chairs in positions of power."

What drove the Cockroach movement?

Content creator Arun Singh, known by his social media handle "TheJhumroo," said that meme culture kept the satire and humor fresh throughout the protests.

"It's the meme culture which fueled this kind of emotion. As millennials, we developed the language of memes as we adapted to the internet culture, but this younger generation was born with memes being their language. This is how they communicate," he told DW.

Singh said that the young protesters are best described as "fearless."

"They don't fear anyone, they don't worry about how they would be perceived and that's what happens when you're absolutely young. That is what is driving their grit," he said.

Mumbai-based comedian Aditi Mittal observes that the fearlessness of the Gen Z protesters comes from them living in a "hyper visible world".

"All of them have 500 followers at a minimum. If something goes up on their stories, it's not going to go vastly ignored," she told DW.

Mittal also thinks that India's Gen Z inherited the "perfect protest."

"The generation prior to ours wanted better infrastructure. We millennials aspired to have a more equal world, ours was a time distinct with, for example, the mistreatment of Muslims. We grew up in that and were constantly gaslit into… 'it's not that bad, it's not happening.' We were also overly forbearing," she told DW. "Gen Z inherited the perfect protest. Education goes beyond religion and secularism. It can resonate, especially for a country like ours where education has been the tool of escape from social class or a financial situation."

Mittal also points out differences between today and the 2019 citizenship law (CAA) protests, one of the last big protests that had challenged the Modi government, and was centered on discrimination against Muslims.

"The anti-CAA protests constantly demanded the perfection of the protesters. Be nice to them [authorities] even as they beat you or hold a gun to you, that was the language spoken to us. But these younger kids don't stand around and wait. They are not tripping over themselves to be perfect," she said.

Getting attention with political humor

Satire is not new to India's politics. For example, caricatures were used as a means to channel anti-colonial anger in Bengal. Political cartoonists like Abu Abraham and R K Laxman challenged censorship brought on by former Prime Minister and Congress leader Indira Gandhi's imposition of a state of emergency that suspended civil liberties between 1975 and 1977.

"Satire is a great way of putting your word across. It's like eating a healthy food, but cooked in an interesting way, which is munchable. Humor has better penetration when it comes to content. It gets more eyeballs," content creator Singh told DW.

Academic and writer Ananya Vajpeyi said that this sense of humor built sympathy with the students and kept the mood light and non-threatening.

"These were young boys and girls who looked tiny, not strong, not threatening, not even articulate sometimes, who had drawn or written something funny on a piece of paper. The violent crackdown backfired immediately because these were not two equal forces facing each other," she told DW.

India's Gen-Z rattles 'brand Modi'

Modi is seen as an image-conscious politician and his 12 years in India's seat of power have been defined by a carefully crafted image that relies heavily on perception management and public relations.

Many of the protesters directly mocked Modi, challenging his brand.

"The whole atmosphere has been so stifled since the anti-CAA protest was shut down. People have been punished for expressing any kind of criticism or dissent. And here you have thousands of students from every corner of the country, just like cockroaches crawling out of the woodwork and making life hell for the Modi establishment," Vajpeyi told DW.

Vajpeyi says the ire against Modi has likely caused "embarrassment" for the prime minister.

"What these kids are saying is like a punch in the stomach for Modi, if he is able to see all this. It's possible that he's being kept from it by those around him, but the opposition sees it," she said. "The rest of the country who is on social media sees it."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Ghana's community service bill: A fix for the prison crisis?
entries.summary: The community service bill offers community service as an alternative to prison sentences, particularly for minor offenses. It's meant to decongest Ghana's prisons and prevent overcrowding once it's signed into law.
entries.content:
July 27, 2026

The community service bill offers community service as an alternative to prison sentences, particularly for minor offenses. It's meant to decongest Ghana's prisons and prevent overcrowding once it's signed into law.

Ghana's parliament recently passed the Community Service Bill, 2026. The piece of legislation is designed to introduce community service as an alternative to custodial sentences for minor offenses. The bill also seeks to ease pressure on the country's overcrowded prisons and reshape how justice is administered for minor crimes.

The legislation establishes a National Community Service Secretariat and provides a legal framework for courts to impose community service in Ghana instead of imprisonment for specified offenses.

According to the government, the move will reduce the financial strain of maintaining prison facilities, which have long suffered from inadequate budgets, high medical costs and chronic congestion.

"If you check the current prison population, overcrowding is over 37%. We have a current population of over 13,000 prisoners. Today the cost of maintaining them, feeding them alone, requires 10 million cedis (€752,000, $859,000)  a quarter," Ghana's Interior Minister, Muntaka Mubarak, who tabled the bill in parliament, told the house during a debate.

Which offenses are covered under the community service bill?

Under the bill, community service applies to offenses punishable by not more than three years' imprisonment, with or without a fine. Courts may also impose community service for offenses that carry fines alone or fines combined with imprisonment.

This means petty crimes such as false publication or traffic offenses could now attract noncustodial penalties.

Legal practitioner Christian Malm Hesse described the bill as "a step in the right direction," noting its potential to reduce prison overcrowding.

He told DW that the bill provides a structured alternative for misdemeanor offenses that previously defaulted to custodial sentences.

However, some Ghanaians believe that its effectiveness will depend on proper categorization of offenses and public education.

According to DW correspondent Eric Mawuena Egbeta, many Ghanaians still need clarity on which offenses qualify.

"An offense which is higher than a misdemeanor would mean that you will not get a community sentence… A lot more persons would need education on it," Egbeta said.

For legal practitioners like Hesse, one key safeguard in the bill is the requirement for a social inquiry report, which helps judges assess an offender's background, circumstances and suitability for community service. Hesse said such measures ensure that sentencing decisions are informed and consistent, reducing the risk of arbitrary application.

Africa's shift toward noncustodial sentencing

Ghana's new passage aligns with a growing trend across Africa, where countries such as Nigeria, Kenya, Zimbabwe, Malawi, Tanzania and Uganda have adopted similar noncustodial sentencing legislation.

International bodies, including the United NationsOffice on Drugs and Crime, have long encouraged alternatives to prison sentences, citing benefits such as reduced recidivism (where a person returns to criminal behavior and is sent back to jail after finishing a past sentence), lower state expenditure and improved community reintegration.

For Ghana, the bill represents the culmination of a decade-long policy process initiated in 2014 by the Ministry of the Interior with support from UNICEF.  The resulting framework aims to modernize justice administration and align national laws with global best practices on restorative justice.

Experts say the bill could be a game-changer for the continent, offering a model for balancing accountability with rehabilitation. By redirecting minor offenders toward community labor, skills development and civic responsibility, Ghana joins a broader African effort to rethink punishment beyond incarceration.

What do Ghanaians think about the bill?

Christabel Success, a Ghanaian journalist, said the law is "most appropriate for minor offenses," but stressed the need for fairness in its application.

"The method of application is what will determine whether it is a good bill or not," she told DW.

"It will help us with our capacity building, nation building and ridding our communities and our environment of waste," Nurah Suglo, an Accra-based resident, told DW.  

"We'd have cleaner cities, cleaner regions and make good use of our labor instead of overcrowding our prisons. People with minor offenses get to also do something that will contribute to the nation as a whole," Success added.

Egbeta, however, noted that crimes classified as second-degree felonies, such as stealing after breaking into a home, remain outside the bill's scope, which may disappoint those hoping for broader reforms. Although Parliament has passed the Community Service Bill, it cannot take effect until President John Dramani Mahama gives his assent.

Despite hailing its passage, Hesse explained that another crucial step for the bill is the creation of a Legislative Instrument (L.I).

"What is left is an L.I. When bills like this are passed, it becomes the secondary legislation under which operations become effective," Hesse said.

This article was adapted from an AfricaLink Podcast. You can listen to the podcast here.

Edited by: Chrispin Mwakideu

entries.title: Fujimori takes charge in Peru amid China, US balancing act
entries.summary: Peru's new president, Keiko Fujimori, has promised more security and investment. As she takes office, she'll have to find space for the South American nation amid Washington and Beijing's geopolitical rivalry.
entries.content:
Peru

Fujimori takes charge in Peru amid China, US balancing act

July 27, 2026

Peru's new president, Keiko Fujimori, has promised more security and investment. As she takes office, she'll have to find space for the South American nation amid Washington and Beijing's geopolitical rivalry.

When Keiko Fujimori steps into the presidential office on Tuesday, she'll bring back a political movement that hasn't been in power for more than a quarter century.

Fujimorism, a mix of neoliberalism, populism and strict government policies, characterized the 1990-2000 presidency of her father, the late Alberto Fujimori. Keiko Fujimori is stepping in amid a climate of social polarization, with promises to deliver more security, economic recovery and improvements in the health and education sectors.

But beyond those domestic projects, Fujimori is taking charge at a time of increased strategic importance for Peru. The country has become one of the key battlegrounds in the growing competition between the United States and China for political influence in South America.

Tough on crime

Fujimori has already signaled that security will be the top priority for her government.

On the agenda: more video surveillance, a stronger police presence, tougher punishment for crimes and organized gangs, and command and control centers across the country. Part of the crackdown includes the construction of four mega-prisons, like those in El Salvador.

Eliana Carlin, a political science expert at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru in Lima, is concerned by how Fujimori's plans will affect human rights.

"Behind [these measures] lie strong ideological positions intended to justify making the police and the armed forces solely subject to military jurisdiction," she said.

In addition to a stronger focus on security, Fujimori has said she intends to advance infrastructure projects, attract private investment, build new schools and hospitals and modernize the country with the help of technology and artificial intelligence.

But delivering on these pledges depends largely on whether the government can find the necessary funds. Infrastructure and essential services continue to face significant deficits. Added to that is the surging crime rate and the threat of the strengthening El Nino weather pattern, which could hit Peru with increased drought, extreme heat, flooding and other climate-related disruptions.

Strategic player in South America

Foreign policy will also be a major challenge for Fujimori's administration. The opening of the Chancay port and logistics hub has turned Peru into a strategic player in regional trade — and made it a central focus in the geopolitical rivalry between Washington and Beijing.

The estimated $3.5 billion (€3 billion) project is part of China's world-spanning Belt ⁠and Road Initiative. Once fully operational, the port is expected to reduce the shipping time between Peru and China from around 40 to about 23 days, turning Chancay into a new gateway to Asia.

Thanks to the port and other investments, China has become Peru's most important trading partner. Bilateral trade between the two countries exceeded $40 billion in 2024, according to official figures. In second place is the US, with nearly $25 billion in trade.

Michael Shifter, an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in Washington teaching Latin American politics, said there's a lot at stake in Peru.

"Beijing has played a very important role in the Peruvian economy for many years, while at the same time the US is seeking to expand its influence. Nowhere is the competition between Beijing and Washington as evident as in Peru," he told DW.

For Shifter, the port at Chancay will be important for both Peru and its regional neighbors. "It will reduce transportation costs and facilitate trade with Asia, particularly with China," he said. "The project has enormous potential for the future of the South American economy."

Part of a planned "bioceanic" corridor between Brazil and Peru, the Pacific hub at Chancay will be connected via rail and road projects to the Atlantic Ocean, facilitating the export of products from all over South America to Asia.

Balancing China, US 'will not be easy'

Fujimori has also announced plans to expand her cooperation with the US, particularly in the areas of security and the fight against organized crime. For Shifter, the challenge will be to maintain the delicate balance between Washington and Beijing.

"Keiko wants to align herself with Washington and avoid tensions with the US. At the same time, China has been indispensable to the Peruvian economy for many years, and the port of Chancay enjoys broad support in Peru. Balancing this relationship will not be easy," he said.

To stay on the US president's good side, Peru's participation in the so-called "Shield of the Americas" will also be key. The alliance, initiated by Donald Trump to combat organized crime, has already welcomed the cooperation of, among others, the right-wing governments of Argentina, Chile, Ecuador and El Salvador.

According to Shifter, involvement in "the 'Shield of the Americas' would also serve to demonstrate a closeness to the Trump administration."

New roll for Peru in Latin America

Fujimori's inauguration comes at a time when conservative forces have gained influence in several Latin American countries. For Shifter, however, Peru's case is unique.

"It's tempting to interpret her election victory as yet another shift to the right in Latin America. But Peru is more complex than that. Keiko Fujimori has shaped Peruvian politics for many years, and the country had already been pursuing a rather pragmatic course," he said.

Political scientist Carlin, however, fully expects a foreign policy shift.

"[Fujimori] has already made it clear that she wants to align more closely with the US and other conservative governments. I think we'll see Peru adopt a tougher foreign policy stance, but I don't think that Peru can do without China," she said. "A break with Beijing would not be realistic."

This article was originally written in Spanish.

entries.title: How India's Gen-Z protesters shifted the political debate
entries.summary: The resignation of India's education minister amounts to a stunning victory for the youth-led "Cockroach" protest movement. The bigger question is if this political momentum turns into a lasting platform for more reform.
entries.content:
India

How India's Gen-Z protesters shifted the political debate

July 27, 2026

The resignation of India's education minister amounts to a stunning victory for the youth-led "Cockroach" protest movement. The bigger question is if this political momentum turns into a lasting platform for more reform.

On Saturday, student protesters embraced, danced and climbed onto barricades as chants of victory echoed across New Delhi's historic Jantar Mantar protest site.

After weeks of demonstrations, marathon negotiations and repeated government refusals, a movement named the "Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)" succeeded in its demand for Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to step down.

The movement began on social media as a satirical activist campaign sparked by leaks of a question sheet for the highly competitive NEET exam in early May.

Along with Pradhan's resignation, the government also agreed to provide the maximum possible compensation to families of students who died by suicide following the NEET paper leak controversy. Additionally, it promised to withdraw criminal cases against protesters, refrain from pursuing future legal action and continue discussions on the CJP's five-point charter for academic examination reform.

The CJP, in turn, announced it was calling off further protest action "in good faith" while added that it would closely monitor whether the government promises were implemented.

"This is a victory of democracy," CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke told thousands of jubilant supporters.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has insisted meeting some of the protest demands reflects responsible governance rather than capitulation.

"Pradhan's resignation is an example of putting students and the nation above political positions," said Home Minister Amit Shah.

However, the resignation of a cabinet minister following public outcry amounts to a rare retreat by Modi's government. Taken together, the concessions mark a remarkable victory for a movement that the government had initially dismissed as little more than a social media campaign.

"Nobody should underestimate student power. Our voice is finally heard. When we stand united, we can achieve many things," Uma Singh, a CJP supporter from the eastern Bihar state who spent days camping in New Delhi, told DW.

Cockroach movement forces a rare BJP retreat

Some 48 hours before Pradhan's resignation, senior Hindu nationalist BJP and government sources had said removing him was not under serious consideration, even as protests continued to grow in Delhi while solidarity demonstrations spread to cities across India.

Earlier concessions, including the removal of 47 National Testing Agency officials, promises of fast-track courts and administrative reshuffles, failed to satisfy protesters.

At the same time, the government faced growing concern that the confrontation would dominate the monsoon session of parliament and hand the opposition a powerful political issue.

Faced with mounting pressure both on the streets and inside parliament, the BJP reversed course.

Indian activist Amrita Johri believes the Cockroach movement's victory amounts to a major shift in political debate in India.

"The movement's significance extends well beyond the resignation of one minister. It showed that a loosely organized generation of young Indians could compel political concessions from a government long regarded as resistant to street pressure," Johri told DW.

"It shifted the debate from examination scandals to larger questions about whether India's institutions are still seen as fair, transparent and accountable. Electoral mandates may confer power, but lasting authority depends on public confidence," she added.

Beyond the immediate political settlement, the government's bigger challenge is rebuilding public trust in institutions that millions of young Indians depend on for opportunity.

Political scientist Gilles Verniers from the Paris-based Sciences Po public research university believes the episode has also exposed a weakness in the BJPs political instincts.

"Modi's usual playbook of staying above the fray, making broad promises and shifting responsibility down the chain failed this time," Verniers told DW.

"The minister's resignation is a clear victory for the protesters and a personal setback for a prime minister who stood by him until the end."

"It exposed a ruling party unprepared for a movement that was neither sectoral nor partisan, and a political class unaccustomed to a generation willing to openly challenge authority rather than defer to it," Verniers added.

BJP normally doesn't budge under pressure

In the past, the Modi government has seldom appeared willing to yield to sustained public pressure.

The closest comparison came during widescale farmers' protests, during which an estimated 700 to 750 protesters died before the government repealed three contentious farm laws in 2021.

Even then, legislation was withdrawn without ministerial accountability. This time, however, a cabinet minister has paid a political price.

The situation has also presented the opposition with evidence that sustained mobilization around issues such as unemployment, education and governance can put the government under pressure.

Senior Congress leader Jairam Ramesh called Pradhan's resignation "a victory for a generation tired of struggling in an unfair and corrupt system," arguing that sustained pressure from students had finally forced the prime minister to withdraw his political backing for the education minister.

The BJP, for its part, argues it acted responsibly to restore confidence in the country's education system and protect students' interests.

Can the protest movement move forward?

The youth-led movement's next test is whether it can convert this political momentum into a lasting platform for institutional reform.

Talks with the government will continue over its five-point examination reform charter, and CJP leaders have warned they will return to the streets if promised changes fail to materialize.

For the government, the challenge is equally significant.

The immediate crisis may have passed, but the government has discovered that a decentralized, youth driven movement can rapidly shape the national political conversation.

Whether the CJP becomes a lasting political force or fades after achieving its immediate goals remains uncertain.

What is no longer in doubt is that it forced one of India's most powerful governments into a concession few believed possible only weeks earlier, reminding both politicians and young voters that organized public pressure can still shape Indian politics.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Germany: Islamist terror attack on Berlin Pride parade triggers political debate
entries.summary: Following the terrorist attack on Berlin's Pride parade, the Christopher Street Day parade, politicians and security experts are demanding consequences.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Islamist terror attack triggers political debate

July 27, 2026

Following the terrorist attack on Berlin's Pride parade, the Christopher Street Day parade, politicians and security experts are demanding consequences.

Berlin remains in shock following the attack on the "Christopher Street Day" (CSD) parade on Saturday. Hundreds of thousands of people had been celebrating peacefully and advocating for the rights of queer individuals — until, around 10 p.m., an attacker drove his vehicle into the crowd in the Tiergarten Park, right in the heart of the city.

One woman was killed and 29 others were injured, some seriously. Authorities quickly said the incident was a terrorist act committed by an Islamist. The suspect initially managed to flee but was later killed by police.

On Sunday afternoon, during a memorial service at St. Mary's Church (Marienkirche), not far from the Brandenburg Gate, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) said: "We will do everything to protect the freedom of our country and our society — everything!" He called out to the mourners: "Stand together, celebrate, and show the joyful face of our open, free society." Yet, right now, no one feels like celebrating.

This sentiment was echoed by the opposition. "Hatred must never triumph," said Luigi Pantisano, leader of the socialist Left Party. "Regardless of whether the hatred stems from religious fanaticism or if the attacks and hostility come from elsewhere," he continued.

The suspect was known to police

The suspected perpetrator was a 21-year-old German national, born to a woman of Lebanese origin. He was known to the police as a sympathizer with the Islamist terrorist militia "Islamic State" (IS) in Syria. In the summer of 2025, he attempted to travel to Syria via Turkey and Lebanon to join IS fighters. However, he was detained in Lebanon, brought back to Germany in November 2025, and placed in pre-trial detention.

He stood trial in Berlin on charges of preparing a serious act of violence. Prosecutors sought a prison sentence of two years and ten months. However, the court released the young man, handing down a suspended sentence of one year and ten months. The IS sympathizer had been free since mid-May of this year — a decision the prosecution appealed.

Although the man's phone was wiretapped for a time, he was not subject to comprehensive surveillance.

At liberty despite clear IS sympathies? That must not happen again, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) said on Sunday: "Part of the review process will be determining whether suspended sentences are actually appropriate in such cases," Dobrindt told public broadcaster ZDF. "It is simply a matter of being able to restrict the freedom of movement of such individuals," Dobrindt concluded.

The main opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) spoke of a total failure of security policy. "If an Islamist 'threat actor' known to the police was able to commit such an act, there must be a thorough investigation into why he was able to move about freely in the first place," said AfD interior policy spokesperson Martin Hess.

Konstantin von Notz of the environmentalist Green Party called for greater powers for security agencies in dealing with violent Islamists and drew a parallel to previous incidents: "It leaves one utterly stunned that this apparently involves yet another 'person of interest' who was already on the authorities' radar," the Green Party politician said.

Criminal prosecution under scrutiny

"What actually happened after his release from prison? With whom did he maintain contact? Even though he was under surveillance, there was clearly a gap here; that is precisely what we need to examine in minute detail — and rest assured, we will," said Sebastian Fiedler of the center-left Social Democratic Party(SPD) which is currently part of the federal government as junior coalition partner to the conservative CDU/CSU bloc.

"Overall, our criminal laws regarding terrorism are too lenient," terrorism expert Peter Neumann of King's College London told public broadcaster ZDF. He noted that prison sentences in Germany are short by European standards, particularly when compared to those in France and the United Kingdom.

However, many experts also point out that it is difficult to maintain comprehensive surveillance on individuals whom German courts have not sentenced to prison. The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency, estimates that there are currently around 420 individuals in Germany classified as "Islamist security threats" — a term referring to people whom authorities believe capable of committing a terrorist act. It remains unclear whether the suspected perpetrator Abdul B.* was among them. Security experts estimate, however, that placing all such individuals under round-the-clock surveillance would completely overwhelm the authorities — especially given that the total number of potentially violent Islamists in Germany is estimated to be significantly higher, at around 9,000 people.

Dirk Peglow, chairman of the Association of German Criminal Investigators (BDK), told the Handelsblatt newspaper on Monday: "In the case of an individual posing such a high level of risk, release from custody must not mean the end of state monitoring." However, Peglow also pointed out that if authorities are expected to monitor particularly dangerous individuals over extended periods, state security and surveillance units must be "appropriately equipped in terms of personnel, technology, and organization"— which, at present, they are not.

The court had ordered the young man to attend a total of 26 appointments at a deradicalization center. Abdul B. had already completed two of these; a third counseling session was scheduled for that Monday. There is widespread criticism now of whether such trainings de facto serve their purpose.

This article has been translated from German.

*DW withholds the full names of perpetrators in order not to increase their publicity and the likelihood of copycat killers.

entries.title: 'Amnesia' about measles risk and low vaccination rates have helped US infections grow
entries.summary: The latest US data show measles cases from January to mid-July 2026 totaled more than all cases in 2025. Experts blame a fall in vaccination and warn that people have forgotten measles can be life-threatening.
entries.content:
July 27, 2026

The latest US data show measles cases from January to mid-July 2026 totaled more than all cases in 2025. Experts blame a fall in vaccination and warn that people have forgotten measles can be life-threatening.

Behind the familiar symptoms of fever and spots is an extremely contagious virus that can cause lasting harm or death. That's the reality of measles.

But many people in the US appear to have forgotten the seriousness of a measles infection, with outbreaks mainly in under-vaccinated communities.

In fact, infections have hit a 35-year high as declining vaccination rates have created growing pockets of susceptible people.

Experts warn that the fading memories of the once-common disease have left too many people unaware of its dangers.

The number of measles cases in the United States up to mid-July 2026 surpassed the total number of cases in 2025. By the week of July 13-19, 2026, the number of reported measles cases was 2,321. By comparison, the total number of US measles cases in 2025 was 2,286, according to the US Measles Tracker run by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. 

What does the rise in measles cases mean?

Johns Hopkins epidemiologist William Moss expects the surge in measles cases to result in the US losing the measles-elimination status it has held since 2000.

"The significance of reaching this milestone is that the US has not been able to stop measles virus transmission or outbreaks as it has in the past," Moss told DW.

Moss said the virus was now spreading "from one susceptible community to another within the US," rather than being limited to infections brought in from abroad.

Measles virus is contagious before spots appear

Measles is the most contagious virus on Earth, spreading far more easily than the common cold. Nine out of 10 non-immune people exposed to the virus will become infected.

Measles spreads through virus-containing droplets released from an infected person's nose, throat and lungs when they breathe, talk or cough. The smallest particles can remain suspended in the air long after the person has left the room.

"You just have to be in somebody's airspace within two hours of them being there," said Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia.

Crucially, people can transmit measles before realizing they are infected.

Patients typically become contagious around four days before the characteristic spots or rash appear.

The combination of airborne particles, extreme contagion and transmission before obvious symptoms allows the virus to exploit even relatively small gaps in vaccination.

Measles complications can emerge years later

In the US, about one in five people with measles are hospitalized.

One in 20 infected children develops pneumonia, while around one in 1,000 develops encephalitis, a form of brain inflammation that can cause permanent brain damage.

Between one and three of every 1,000 infected children die from respiratory or neurological complications.

"We had two unvaccinated children — a healthy little six-year-old, a healthy little eight-year-old — die of measles this past year," Offit told DW.

Both died with pneumonia. "It's like dying of suffocation," he said. "It's a terrible way to die."

Among those who survive, the harm can persist long after the fever and spots disappear.

Measles can suppress the immune system for years, erasing some of the protection it had previously developed against other viruses and bacteria.

Another delayed complication is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a rare but fatal degenerative brain disease that can appear up to 10 years after the original infection.

"Children get infected, they get better, they're fine," Offit said. "And then five years later, seven years later, they come in with a deterioration in handwriting skills, deterioration in personality and then they descend into a vegetative state and die."

Has the danger of measles been forgotten?

Vaccination pushed measles out of everyday life in the US. But that success has also weakened public understanding of why vaccination is necessary.

"We've not just largely eliminated measles from our country; we've eliminated the memory of measles," Offit said.

"The most serious complications of measles are relatively rare and only become apparent when there is a large number of cases," said Moss. "Unfortunately, the increasing number of measles cases in the US will once again teach us that this is not always a harmless childhood infection."

Katelyn Jetelina, an epidemiologist who publishes a Substack newsletter called "Your Local Epidemiologist," said falling vaccination rates reflected a "general amnesia about these diseases," falsehoods on social media and a wider loss of trust in institutions.

"The outbreaks remain among under-vaccinated communities," Jetelina said. "There are unvaccinated pockets all around the nation. All it takes is a spark for this disease to spread like wildfire in those pockets."

Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

entries.title: FIFA boss Infantino takes aim at World Cup critics
entries.summary: In a strongly worded open statement, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has hit out at those he says were too "consumed by hate and criticism" to enjoy the tournament. Infantino brushed off a number of corruption concerns.
entries.content:
United States of America

FIFA boss Infantino takes aim at World Cup critics

July 27, 2026

In a strongly worded open statement, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has hit out at those he says were too "consumed by hate and criticism" to enjoy the tournament. Infantino brushed off a number of corruption concerns.

Gianni Infantino is not a man used to apologizing. And even though he said sorry three times on the second slide of a 15-page Instagram post, that remains the case.

"To everyone who missed our beautiful game, the emotions, the celebrations, the laughter, the crying, the deception, and the joy. To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents, and parents come together for the beautiful game, I say sorry that the matches are now over and sorry that you missed all that joy and togetherness. Sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," read a missive from the FIFA president posted on FIFA's website, his personal Instagram account, and FIFA's online and social channels. Comments were turned off.

The Swiss executive went on to claim that the World Cup, had brought "no violence, no incidents, 100% safety and security, only joy and happiness!” The exclamation mark was not the only part of the message reminiscent of US President Donald Trump's communication style.

Infantino claims to have 'united' Iran and USA

"While you spread hatred, we worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war. Iran entered the United States without incident or conflict," Infantino wrote.

In fact, Iran were treated differently to any of the other 47 teams at the World Cup. They were forced to stay in Mexico and travel to their games in the US and had further last minute restrictions imposed on them after their matches.

Iran head coach Amir Ghalenoei said his team were the "most oppressed" at the World Cup after the travel chaos came on top of several support staff being denied visas.

Travel bans and visa refusals were a running theme of the tournament. Trump's travel bans denied entry to fans from several participating countries, including Haiti, Senegal, Iran and the Ivory Coast, which faced varying levels of bans or restrictions.

Furthermore Somali referee Omar Artan was denied entry to the US due to unsubstantiated US government claims that he had an "association with suspected members of terror organizations," despite the fact that he held a diplomatic passport and the had been issued the correct visa.

FIFA and UEFA split becoming clearer

But, Infantino said, people should instead be looking at FIFA's successes.

"You mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world. Because football unites the world, and it was demonstrated impressively this summer," he added.

Infantino's relationship with Trump has been another bone of contention for many. After awarding Trump the newly introduced FIFA Peace Prize in December, Trump admitted to phoning Infantino to lobby on behalf of US striker Folarin Balogun, whose red card ban was suspended in a near-unprecedented move at a World Cup.

"Indeed, 'arguable' referees' decisions or 'strange" disciplinary rulings such as for instance potentially mistaken red or yellow cards or subsequent decisions not to ban players in certain situations are routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide," Infantino wrote.

However, FIFA's own rules state that red card bans at World Cups cannot be appealed or overturned, which Balogun's, in a World Cup context at least, was.

"It's curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticizing," continued Infantino in what appeared to be a shot at European governing body UEFA, which publicly said FIFA had "crossed a red line" in the Balogun incident. UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin failed to attend the World Cup final, a move widely understood to have been in protest — with FIFA and its biggest continental association at loggerheads.

Trump wants Infantino as UN Secretary-General

Shortly after the final, Trump recommended Infantino for the post of secretary-general of the United Nations, which is up for grabs at the end of this year.

But, despite the thoughts of his "close friend," Infantino looks set to remain at FIFA, where he is expected to be elected unopposed once again next year. In Sunday's message he praised his own organization for delivering despite the further criticism of hydration breaks and FIFA breaking their own rules to extend halftime in the final.

"To the pens and papers, to all the screens, may you find love and peace where the people behind you couldn't.

May you find peace; we at FIFA have found ours and we deliver it, by delivering the most outstanding FIFA World Cup. May football rise above all hate."

It is a message that the Iranian team, Haitian fans and Omar Artan may well have shared, had they been allowed to enjoy the World Cup with the same freedoms as Infantino.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold
